passages.paragraph_text: Yeah, I would agree in most cases. You know, there's something else I want to throw out about China, and I've experienced this a lot in just seeing friends, you know, start hardware companies. And I'm an advisor for a few companies that are out there who get into hardware manufacturing and they go, oh, you know, we're just going to go to China, and China will fix it. So we'll send them the prototype. China will fix it, and it will magically become a product. And so there's sort of this void of people that want to manufacture their own hardware just, you know, dumping stuff onto a factory and just assuming that it's going to be done right. And, you know, a factory – most factories, you know, will have some engineering, some real engineers on staff. But it doesn't mean that they're any better than anybody else. So that's something I just wanted to kind of mention is that you always need to keep an eye on your product, even if you do send it offshore. You know, if a company might – you know, a factory might swap in different capacitors because they have a relationship with the company. Yeah, the cheaper – Yeah, exactly. And then you run into the failure problem. You know, what was that? That PDK, I think, had capacitors that were failing. Or, you know, maybe a factory has a broker relationship with some broker that's getting counterfeit parts or crap parts. Yeah, some gray market, yeah. Yeah, and that happens a lot unless you have that face-to-face contact and the client knows – or the factory knows that, you know, you're a serious client. And most people aren't going to go to China and introduce themselves. So there's a lot of risk there that kind of will come later, right? If your product ends up – they substitute parts and then three months down the line products start failing, that's going to be a complete nightmare to try to, you know, reverse engineer the problem and then work backwards.
